article_text:
Join us from 22 October to support the AAA’s contribution to art, society and community.

Asia Art Archive (AAA)’s annual fundraiser returns on 22 October, with more than 50 works – from around the world, generously donated by artists, galleries and private individuals – up for auction online and in person. Proceeds will support AAA’s ongoing work to preserve and share contemporary art-histories in Asia, while strengthening the knowledge, resources and capacity needed to ensure that these histories remain accessible for generations to come.

Highlights from this year’s auction include work by Salima Hashmi, Chen Qingqing, Christopher K. Ho, Donny Cheng, Huang Rui, Mok Yat-san, Qiu Xiaofei, Ashmina Ranjit, Anju Dodiya, Jakkai Siributr, Wong Sze Wai, Xu Bing, Young-Hae Chang, Heavy Industries, Yu Peng, and more.

AAA is a Hong Kong-based independent non-profit organisation ‘initiated in response to the urgent need to document and make accessible the multiple recent histories of art in the region’. With an archive of over 140,000 records, AAA has one of the most valuable collections of material on art, freely available on its website and in its onsite library. The organisation’s ethos centres on expanding knowledge through research, residency and educational programmes.

And rarely more so than in this, the Archive’s 25th anniversary year. In August, AAA launched the Archiving Handbook , a practical guide designed to support artists and art spaces in preserving their own creative legacies. Introducing fundamental archival principles and workflows, the handbook builds on seven hands-on Archiving Workshops held in Hong Kong, Macau, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Hangzhou, Riyadh and Ho Chi Minh City. These workshops brought together practical exercises and discussions spanning technical applications and theoretical approaches. The handbook is now freely available online for independent exploration.

This year has also seen the initiation of a two-year project New Archive: Hong Kong at the Forefront of Preserving Arts and Culture , which will extend AAA’s role as a platform for professional training, research, technological experimentation and knowledge exchange in digital archiving. Through internships, on-the-job training, international exchanges, expert-led workshops, and educational resources, the initiative will prepare a new generation of archivists and cultural professionals for preservation in the digital age. The New Archive project is supported by the Arts Capacity Development Funding Scheme.

Join us from 22 October in supporting AAA’s contribution to the history of art, society and community.

AAA’s 2026 Annual Fundraiser is supported by Altaya Wines, Christie’s Hong Kong, Chubb, Jebsen and WTW | Willis, along with venue sponsor, H Queen’s and media partners who, alongside ArtReview Asia , include Art & Market , Ocula , Tatler Hong Kong , The Artling and The Value .

Venue H Queen’s, 11/F, 80 Queen’s Road Central, Hong Kong

Auction Preview 22–24 October, 11am–7pm 25 October, 11am–3pm

Media Tour 22 October, 3–4pm Please contact Christy Li at christy@aaa.org.hk to RSVP

Opening Reception 22 October, 6–8pm

Online Auction 22 October, 10:30am to 6 November, 10:30pm via aaa2026auction.com

article_text:
Série original foi criada por Mel Brooks e Buck Henry.

Um dos agentes secretos mais queridos da televisão está voltando. Uma nova adaptação de “ Agente 86 ” está em desenvolvimento pela Warner, com o comediante John Mulaney cotado para interpretar o protagonista Maxwell Smart (via Deadline ).

A série original de “Agente 86” foi criada por Mel Brooks e Buck Henry e exibida nos EUA entre 1965 e 1970. Funcionando como uma paródia de “James Bond”, a trama acompanha os agentes Maxwell Smart (Agente 86) e a Agente 99 trabalhando para a agência Control, que trava uma batalha constante contra a organização maligna Kaos. Durante os episódios, Smart frequentemente leva a melhor sobre a Kaos graças a cacarecos como o icônico sapatofone, apesar de sua aparente incompetência.

Em 1980, “Agente 86” ganhou um filme com o retorno do elenco original, com outro longa para televisão sendo lançado em 1989. Em 1995, um revival da série original rendeu apenas sete episódios. Em 2008, a Warner lançou uma adaptação para o cinema estrelada por Steve Carell, Anne Hathaway, Alan Arkin e Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson.

O desenvolvimento da nova adaptação ainda está em estágios iniciais, com Seth Grahame-Smith, de “Truque de Mestre 3”, escrevendo o roteiro. Chuck Roven e Andrew Lazar, que produziram o longa de 2008, também produzem o novo filme.

Ainda não há previsão de estreia para o novo “Agente 86”.

article_text:
少女漫画が飛躍的な進化を遂げた1970年代、その中心には三人の漫画家、萩尾望都・山岸凉子・大和和紀の存在がありました。 国立新美術館 では、彼女らの画業をたどる展覧会 「少女漫画・インフィニティ 萩尾望都×山岸凉子×大和和紀 三人展」 が、10月28日から2027年2月8日まで開催されます。

国立の美術館で開催される初の大規模な少女漫画展となる本展。美しいカラーイラストや名場面の原画、さらに貴重な資料の数々などを通じて、その奥深い表現世界に迫ります。※カラー作品は前期・後期の展示替えあり

萩尾望都×山岸凉子×大和和紀の三人展「少女漫画・インフィニティ」で原画など800点超を展示。六本木・国立新美術館で10月開幕

少女漫画界を代表する3作家の画業をたどる。会期は10月28日〜2027年2月8日

本展のチケットをTokyo Art Beatの有料会員限定で、抽選で2組4名様にプレゼントします。

応募方法

応募フォームに必要事項を記入 期間：10月16日〜10月30日 23:59 👉応募フォームは こちら ＊当選者への発送は11月中を予定しています

article_text:
キース・ヘリングの「幻の壁画」付き高級ロフトが約40億円で売り出し中。壁画だけで建物以上の価値？

キース・ヘリングの壁画が残るニューヨークの3層メゾネットが、2500万ドル（約39億5900万円）で売りに出されている。壁画は長年にわたり壁板の裏に隠されていたが、2007年の改装工事で再発見された。

ニューヨーク の不動産市場では、専用ジムや屋上プールなど、魅力的な付帯設備が物件の価値を大きく押し上げることがある。では、そこに キース・ヘリング の壁画までついていたらどうだろうか。現在、そんな物件が2500万ドル（約39億5900万円）で売りに出されている。

ニューヨーク・タイムズ紙によれば、この物件は7つの寝室を備えたロフトで、ヘリングが1979年に制作した壁画が室内の壁や天井、支柱に直接 描かれている 。つまり、アートが物件に付属している（あるいは物件がアートに付属している）と言っても過言ではない。

広さおよそ740平方メートルにおよぶこの3層メゾネットは、1896年に完成したネオルネッサンス建築、アメリカン・スレッド・ビルディングの一室だ。ヘリングの作品に加え、9つのバスルームや試写室、ジム、サウナが備え付けられており、天井高は約8.5メートルに及ぶ。

この壁画は、スクール・オブ・ビジュアル・アーツ在学中のヘリングによって制作された。同校は当時、この建物の一部を学生向けの展示スペースとして使用していた。靴墨とアルコールを混ぜて描かれたこの作品には、のちにヘリングの代名詞となるグラフィティのような人や物の形が描かれている。

しかし、スクール・オブ・ビジュアル・アーツが撤退した後、このスペースはレストランに改装され、壁画は壁板の裏に隠されてしまった。それから数十年にわたり人目に触れることはなく、再びその存在が明らかになったのは2007年のことだった。

壁画を発見したのは、当時の改装に携わっていたニューヨークの建築家、トッド・エルンストだ。エルンストはニューヨーク・マガジンの取材に対し、発見時の驚きを「古代エジプトの墓を発見したかのよう」と 語っている 。水溶性の塗料で描かれたこの作品は、スプリンクラーの配管のすぐ近くにあったにもかかわらず、奇跡的に無傷で残っていた。

この物件はその後、人材採用企業を率いるアダム・ゾイアの手に渡り、2年がかりで改装工事が行われた。改装に際しては、不測の事態から壁画を保護するため、その前にバーカウンターを設置している。ゾイアはニューヨーク・タイムズ紙のインタビューに対し「署名のない壁画をひと目見て、ヘリングの作品だと確信しました」と語った。また、作品の真正性はキース・ヘリング財団によって証明されているという。

この壁画は、鉄の柱や梁、天井、そして周囲の壁面へと広がっている。こうした建物と一体化した作品の価値について、ニューヨークのギャラリストであるジェン・シンガーは、ニューヨーク・タイムズ紙に対し、「サイトスペシフィックな性質をもっているため、物件と切り離して価値を評価することは不可能に近い」と語っている。通常の絵画とは異なり、壁画だけを取り外して売却することが難しいからだ。一方、ゾイアは作品の潜在的な価値について強気な姿勢を見せ、「もし作品を取り外すことができたなら、おそらく物件そのものよりも価値があるでしょう」と同紙に語っている。

現時点でこの物件は、トローヴ・パートナーズを通じて 売りに出されている 。（翻訳：編集部）

ファッションフォトグラファー、クレイグ・マクディーン（Craig McDean）の写真展が、東京・千駄ヶ谷のUNDER R TOKYOで開催される。会期は2026年10月23日から11月6日まで。マクディーンが伝説的なDucatiのモーターサイクルを撮り下ろした新作を展示するほか、同名写真集の発売、UNDER Rとのコラボレーションによるアパレルコレクションも展開される。

1990年代初頭、『i-D』や『The Face』といったカルチャー誌で頭角を現したマクディーン。その後はシャネル、ジル サンダ－、カルバン・クラインをはじめとするブランドの広告キャンペーンやエディトリアルを数多く手がけ、現代のファッションフォトグラフィーを代表する写真家のひとりとして活動してきた。

今回、マクディーンがカメラを向けたのは、Ducatiを象徴する歴史的モデル「750 Supersport Green Frame」。1970年代初頭、同社のチーフデザイナー、ファビオ・タリオーニによって開発された750cc Vツインエンジン搭載のレーシングマシンをルーツとし、1972年のイモラ200マイルレースではデビュー戦で1位と2位を独占。その後、市販モデルとしてわずか401台が生産され、現在も世界のコレクターを魅了する存在となっている。

マクディーンは本プロジェクトで、希少な2台のDucatiと向き合い、そのフォルムやディテール、機械としての構造とクラフトマンシップを写真として記録した。ファッションにおいて身体や衣服、プロダクトを独自の視覚言語へと変換してきた写真家が、モーターサイクルという工業製品をどのようなイメージへと昇華させるのか。写真、デザイン、ファッション、モーターカルチャーが交差する展示となる。

さらにUNDER Rとのコラボレーションアイテムとして、マクディーンの写真を配したTシャツ（8800円）とロングスリーブTシャツ（1万2100円）も登場。

タイトル

Craig McDean Photo Exhibition at UNDER R TOKYO

場所

UNDER R TOKYO（東京都渋谷区千駄ヶ谷2-6-3 1F）

会期

2026年10月23日（金）〜11月6日（金）

時間

11:00〜19:30

休み

無し

料金

無料

URL

https://ronherman.jp/underr

"paragraph", "text": "“我认识卢卡斯很多年了，我很喜欢他的作品。当你找到一个做类似事情的艺术家时，就像是建立了一个家庭。我们都通过设计研究和材料进行创作，并且两人都接受过diseño del proyecto（项目设计）的培训。项目本身就是作品这一理念对我们建筑师来说非常自然。他对材料的研究是回答自己问题的一种方式，我在自己的工作中也发现了类似的情况。但当我看到他的作品时，我也意识到我们有多么不同：在他的作品中有着强烈的工业设计痕迹。我也接受过两个工业设计工坊的培训，广义上的工业设计仍然是我研究的很大一部分。相反，家具设计在十年前曾让我着迷，但今天它不再是我同样投入的领域。”", "“在过去的几年里，我用机器制作了作品，但与此同时我继续制作陶瓷和其他手工制品。对我来说，这是同一种情况：当我都不知道该怎么做时，我才对做某事感兴趣。建造一台在无限循环中重复相同动作的机器，与制作一块圆形砖并没有太大区别：我先画出来，然后用3D建模，在它存在之前我必须经历许多步骤。展出的《Circular Column of Hollow Bricks》（2026）正是诞生于这个过程。有趣的是，我的机器产生的错误多于‘精确’结果，至少根据机器的标准来看是这样。它的行为不像普通机器。从这个意义上说，我的第一个项目《Attempts》和这些最新作品谈论的是同一件事：失败。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从《Attempt to Draw a "“这是我一生中最美好的两个月。米兰接纳了我，并给予我创作的时间和空间，这对于艺术家而言是一份馈赠。我通过这座城市的日常节奏来发现它：在街上、在工作室里，甚至在Esselunga超市的过道里，我在那儿花了太多时间……在这里我感觉像在家一样。”", "translated": true}]

article_text:
A Buenos Aires, gli edifici in attesa di demolizione vengono spesso sigillati murandone porte e finestre con mattoni: facciate cieche, destinate a durare pochi anni. In questa conversazione l’architetto e artista argentino Ignacio Unrrein ci racconta come queste facciate siano diventate, nel suo lavoro, soglie temporanee e opere sul fallimento e sul ritorno, fino alla riscoperta delle sue radici italiane. L’occasione è Still Past , la doppia personale con Lucas Simões , che inaugura la nuova sede milanese di ORMA : una mostra su memoria, stratificazione e materia che apre un dialogo destinato a proseguire a Torino, ad Artissima.

Hai descritto l’architettura come un modo di occupare lo spazio tra gli opposti, tra il costruire e il distruggere. Quando realizzi il modello in scala di un edificio esistente, come la facciata murata di Tucumán 3238 , stai progettando o ricordando?

«Direi entrambe le cose. Una facciata murata contraddice lo scopo principale dell’architettura, e in particolare dell’architettura moderna, che cerca di comprendere e abitare lo spazio interno. All’Università di Buenos Aires il pensiero architettonico moderno era molto influente, quindi pensavo sempre ad abitare l’interno. Poi, attraverso questo processo, ho capito che la facciata murata era anche un invito ad abitare l’esterno. Queste facciate ricordano l’architettura che andrà perduta, perché durano due o tre anni prima di scomparire. In questo senso sono un’opera anti-patrimoniale, ma anche una forma di progetto: l’idea di un’altra architettura possibile».

La tua ricerca di dottorato ha dato un nome a questo territorio, Artiarquitectura . Quali artisti l’hanno plasmato e hanno influenzato di più la tua pratica?

«Ho studiato molti artisti che si sono confrontati con l’architettura, dagli anni Cinquanta a oggi, ma i primi nomi che mi vengono in mente sono Rachel Whiteread, Gordon Matta-Clark, Gregor Schneider e il gruppo Stalker. Leggere di Francesco Careri, uno dei fondatori di Stalker, ha segnato un prima e un dopo: la sua teoria mi ha permesso di abbracciare un altro modo di intendere l’architettura. L’ho conosciuto nel 2018, in occasione di una collettiva al MACRO di Roma. La mia tesi esplora il confine tra architettura e arte. Volevo comprendere entrambe le pratiche, ma anche il punto in cui convergono, uno spazio liminale che si potrebbe considerare una disciplina a sé. Né arte pura, né architettura pura. Artiarquitectura è il nome che ho dato a quest’area».

In Still Past esponi accanto a Lucas Simões, anche lui formatosi come architetto. Cosa condividono le vostre pratiche, e dove si separano?

«Conosco Lucas da molti anni e amo il suo lavoro. Quando trovi un artista che fa qualcosa di simile, è come creare una famiglia. Entrambi lavoriamo attraverso la ricerca progettuale e i materiali, e ci siamo formati entrambi nel diseño del proyecto , la progettazione. L’idea che il progetto stesso sia l’opera è molto naturale per noi architetti. La sua ricerca sui materiali è un modo per rispondere alle sue domande, e io ritrovo situazioni simili nel mio lavoro. Ma quando guardo le sue opere mi rendo anche conto di quanto siamo diversi: nel suo lavoro c’è una forte presenza del design industriale. Anch’io mi sono formato in due laboratori di design industriale, e il design industriale, inteso in senso ampio, fa ancora molto parte della mia ricerca. Il design d’arredo, invece, dieci anni fa mi affascinava, ma oggi non è qualcosa in cui mi senta altrettanto coinvolto».

Il tuo lavoro precedente si basava sulla manualità, e hai usato persino la tua stessa pelle, con i tatuaggi. Ora Cascoteras è una macchina, e le nuove colonne in mostra nascono da stampi progettati in 3D. Cosa cambia quando il tentativo viene affidato a una macchina? Una macchina può fallire come fallisce una mano?

«Negli ultimi anni ho realizzato opere con le macchine, ma parallelamente ho continuato a fare ceramiche e altri pezzi artigianali. Per me è la stessa situazione: mi interessa fare qualcosa quando non so come farla. Costruire una macchina che ripete la stessa azione in un loop infinito non è così diverso dal realizzare un mattone circolare: prima lo disegno, poi lo modello in 3D, e poi devo attraversare molti passaggi prima che esista. La Circular Column of Hollow Bricks (2026) in mostra nasce proprio da questo processo. E la cosa divertente è che la mia macchina produce più errori che risultati “esatti”, almeno secondo i criteri di una macchina. Non si comporta come una macchina normale. In questo senso il mio primo progetto, Attempts , e questi ultimi lavori parlano della stessa cosa: il fallimento».

Da Attempt to Draw a Line a Tapiar Buenos Aires c’è un gesto ricorrente: l’inventario impossibile. Hai censito ogni facciata murata della città, 13.036 piscine, 729 stampe e 211 parole. L’archivio è il filo che attraversa il tuo lavoro?

«Forse, ma non ci penso. Nel mio caso l’archivio è uno strumento. Mi sono sempre trovato a mio agio nel creare archivi di ogni tipo. Probabilmente viene dalla mia formazione di architetto. È più una metodologia che una scelta consapevole. Per questo amo il lavoro di Gregor Schneider: mentre costruiva la sua casa dentro la casa, ha cercato di catalogare rigorosamente ogni modifica, e poi si è reso conto che era impossibile. La sua opera è diventata proprio quell’impossibilità… Credo di cercare qualcosa di simile».

Ignacio Unrrein, Untitled, dal progetto Tapiar Buenos Aires [Murare Buenos Aires], 2021. Ph: Estrella Herrera. Hai la cittadinanza italiana, e gran parte di Buenos Aires è stata costruita da muratori italiani emigrati. Cosa significa riportare questi mattoni a Milano? Still Past è anche un ritorno personale?

«Mi emoziona un po’. La famiglia di mia madre veniva da Castelsaraceno, in Basilicata, quella di mio padre dalla Germania. Come tante persone a Buenos Aires, sono nato dall’incontro di culture diverse, e la storia della mia famiglia mi ha sempre interessato molto. Condivido tutto il processo di produzione con mia madre al telefono, e per lei significa molto. Per me è come vivere un sogno. Non so spiegare cosa provo quando vado in bici dall’appartamento alla galleria. È incredibile quanto il mio corpo si senta a suo agio qui; è quasi soprannaturale. Capisco l’italiano, anche se non l’ho mai studiato. Quando io e mia madre siamo saliti a Castelsaraceno, lei era completamente bloccata, ed ero io a tradurre per lei. Non ho mai studiato la lingua, ma lo farò».

E Milano? Hai già esposto a Roma e a Venezia, ma questa è la prima volta che vivi e produci in Italia.

«Sono stati due dei mesi più belli della mia vita. Milano mi ha accolto e mi ha dato il tempo e lo spazio per produrre, che per un artista è un dono. Ho scoperto la città attraverso i suoi ritmi quotidiani: per strada, in studio, persino tra le corsie dell’Esselunga, dove passo fin troppo tempo… Qui mi sento a casa».

article_text:
Fatalism, self-determination and imagination all gently wrestle for control of the narrative(s) in “ Beach Fictions ,” an enchanting and subtly profound diptych that follows one young woman through two diverging versions of the same day — saying much in the process about the voices, inner and otherwise, that we grant most control in our lives, for better or worse. Though its structuring principle of a single day playing out twice consecutively to differing effect (as opposed to braiding its alternate timelines like “Sliding Doors” or “Blind Chance”) explicitly recalls Hong Sangsoo’s “Right Now, Wrong Then,” this chicly poised debut feature by fellow South Korean Lim Hayeon has a style, tone and outlook of its own, maintained with impressive control over a surprisingly breezy-feeling 145 minutes.

Related Stories

'Nick Cannon @ Night' Podcast Moves to BET, Will Relaunch as a Weekly TV Talk Show (EXCLUSIVE)

One of the real discoveries in this year’s main competition at the Busan Film Festival , “Beach Fictions” should have little difficulty charming other programmers on the international fest circuit following its world premiere — while only its running time, manageable but unexpectedly robust for a film this light on its feet, presents an obstacle to global arthouse distribution, or at least specialist streaming exposure. Either way, this graduation project (produced by the Korean Academy of Film Arts) announces its writer-director-editor as one to watch, should her future films match this one’s warmth and formal elegance; in only her second big-screen outing after years of TV work, winsome lead Hansol Park also feels like a breakout talent.

“Beach Fictions” pulls you in from its first iridescent frame, as Sinuk Park’s camera glides serenely from a bejeweled nighttime view of Incheon through the chattery hubbub of a mood-lit restaurant where Tae-ju (Park), seen only from behind, is dining with friends, their conversation seemingly more animated than hers. Even without the detached voiceover — which turns out to belong to perceptive novelist Ewha (Sujeong Ye), describing the superficial response of Tae-ju’s friends to an anecdote she shares — we’d sense her loneliness amid company. Later, when her friends abandon her at the table to smoke outside, she’s crushed to find them gossiping about her; shortly afterwards, in a never-rains-but-pours development, she breaks up with her casual boyfriend Hyun-jin after he expresses scant interest in taking the relationship further.

With her social life in tatters and a world of her anxieties realized, Tae-ju rashly skips town, heading for the tranquil coastal guesthouse of another friend. On the train there, she encounters Ewha, whom we’ve already seen observing her from afar at the restaurant, and confides in the kindly, silver-haired older woman — who says Tae-ju resembles the protagonist of the novel she’s currently writing. But is she the writer’s inspiration or her creation, an incomplete fiction who has somehow taken on an agency of her own? From here on out, the authorship of Tae-ju’s life is ambiguous, as well as constantly in flux, buffeted by the whims and suggestions of others, as well as by her own impulses.

In the sleepy beach town, she meets and is immediately entranced by charismatic street magician Manhyuk (Kim Wookyum, delightful), only to later be warned off him by her hostess, who claims he’s a local lothario and sometime sex worker. A day in his company turns sour but when, in the film’s deftly shuffled second half, she meets him in slightly different circumstances, and the day’s events take on a different chain of connections, the potential romantic outcome differs too.

Her nascent relationship with Manhyuk is the chief variable of Tae-ju’s two stories, but other, slighter factors push it this way and that: a water-damaged phone in need of repair; a hangout with fellow guesthouse patrons that echoes or corrects her earlier social fallout; and a consultation with a psychic, recommended by Ehwa, whose counsel also shifts her fate. The contrasts between the two tales are never drastic; the gradations are sometimes as fine as those between warm and cool melancholy. The camerawork is consistently, richly sun-flooded, but some compositions isolate Tae-ju more than others; Wonhong Lee’s delicate jazz piano score can similarly tilt a situation from cozy to nervy.

But both gently lolloping narratives hold the attention, in large part thanks to Park’s deeply sympathetic performance as Hae-ju, simultaneously played as a fragile, will-o’-the-wisp go-alonger — or perhaps just an author’s as-yet-unformed blank canvas — and a wounded flesh-and-blood human now guarding her emotions more carefully. It’s a canny turn completely in synch with Lim’s complex, metatextual script, which brims with ideas about the fictional construction process, as well the real-life bind felt by vulnerable young women expected to bend to others’ desires and expectations. Is life itself not just a series of drafts and redrafts, with notes we either learn from or don’t, our characters never not in progress? Wry and wise and happy-sad, “Beach Fictions” crosses nothing out, alive to all possibilities.

article_text:
Doha Film Festival , which takes place from Nov. 19 to 27, has unveiled its Gala Screenings and Special Screenings programs, which include James Gray ’s thriller “Paper Tiger.”

Also selected are “Edward Said: Between Worlds,” Maiken Baird’s documentary exploring the life and legacy of the Palestinian American scholar; Bruno Dumont’s “Red Rocks,” which offers a perspective on childhood, freedom and imagination; Jeffrey Walker’s family adventure “Fing!”; “Life Support,” Daniele Rugo’s documentary about international medical volunteers working alongside Palestinian colleagues in Gaza; Ginevra Elkann’s atmospheric drama “The Roses of Marrakech,” where an unexpected arrival unsettles the carefully ordered lives of those who inhabit it; Ali El Arabi’s debut feature “52 Blue,” about a young man’s journey to Qatar World Cup to meet his idol, Lionel Messi; Rami Kodeih’s thriller “Furies”; and “Artou,” an immersive film by Abderrahmane Sissako.

Related Stories

Fatma Hassan Alremaihi, CEO of Doha Film Institute and director of Doha Film Festival, said: “Our Gala and Special Screenings will bring audiences together through films that move, surprise, and spark conversation. From gripping dramas and timely documentaries to stories filled with humor, adventure and discovery, the selection celebrates the courage to question what we take for granted and find dignity and truth in the complexity of human experience. Audiences will leave the cinema with new perspectives, questions to reflect on, and stories that stay with them long after the final frame.”

Popular on Variety

Three of the films in the lineup were supported by Film Committee at Media City Qatar, underlining the reach of Qatar’s burgeoning industry. These were “Paper Tiger,” “Furies,” and “Artou.”

Gala Screenings “Edward Said: Between Worlds” (U.S./Qatar) by Maiken Baird is set 23 years after the death of Palestinian American scholar, musician and intellectual Edward Said, who revisits the untold history of Palestine in his own words. The film offers an intimate portrait of a defining intellectual voice while examining the enduring question of who has the right to tell their own story. (Middle East Premiere)

“Fing!” (Australia/U.K.) by Jeffrey Walker is about Myrtle Meek who has everything she could ever want, yet for her 12th birthday she demands a Fing. Nobody knows what a Fing is, but her doting parents agree to the request, sending her father on a journey to a lost jungle to find one. (International Premiere)

“Furies” (Lebanon/Brazil) by Rami Kodeih follows determined single mother Maro a year after Lebanon’s economic collapse, who needs her savings to pay for her younger sister Dalia’s life-saving surgery, but when the bank refuses to release the money, the sisters devise a daring, all-night heist to reclaim what is rightfully theirs. (MENA Premiere)

“Paper Tiger” (U.S.) by James Gray is set in 1980s New York, following two brothers whose pursuit of the American Dream draws them into a scheme that seems too good to be true. As they navigate the dangerous world of the Russian mafia, corruption and violence threaten their family, testing their integrity and the loyalties that bind them. (MENA Premiere)

“Red Rocks” (Portugal/France/Italy/Spain/Qatar) by French auteur Bruno Dumont captures a summer on the French Riviera through the fearless adventures of rival gangs of children involving daredevil cliff-jumping competitions. (MENA Premiere)

Special Screenings “Artou” (France/Mauritania/Luxembourg/Qatar), the first 360° immersive film by Abderrahmane Sissako follows three sisters and three brothers on their journey from Europe to Mauritania to fulfill the last wish of their father to be laid to rest beside his father in his native village. (Middle East Premiere)

“Life Support” (U.K./Qatar) by Daniele Rugo is set in Gaza post October 2023, when the city is sealed off from the world with international doctors among the few able to enter its hospitals to volunteer. Filmed largely on the doctors’ phones, the film offers an intimate account of the people striving to preserve life amid a devastating humanitarian crisis. (MENA Premiere)

“The Roses of Marrakech” (Le Rose Di Marrakech) (Italy) by Ginevra Elkann is about Leila, the devoted housekeeper of Madame Isabelle, who lives in a luxurious estate. When her sister arrives unexpectedly with news of a past Leila has long buried, the tranquillity of the estate begins to fracture, revealing the secrets and unresolved histories beneath its seemingly timeless surface. (Middle East Premiere)

“52 Blue” (India/Egypt/U.S.) by Ali El Arabi is a coming-of-age drama that tells the story of Ashish, a reclusive young man set on meeting his idol, Lionel Messi, at the World Cup in Qatar. Lying to his family, he embarks on a journey that leads him from the peaceful and sheltered bubble of his rural Kerala home to a job as a stadium worker. (MENA Premiere)

article_text:
The Whitney Museum in New York has hired Nolan Jimbo as the Arnhold Associate Curator, a role most recently held by Rujeko Hockley. He will start in the role on November 16.

Jimbo is currently an assistant curator at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Chicago, where he started in 2021 as a curatorial fellow. During his tenure at the MCA Chicago, he has organized solo exhibitions for Gregory Bae, which was on view in 2022, the year after the artist’s death; Kenzi Shiokava, the artist’s first institutional survey; and Mike Cloud, which is a nominee for the 2026 ARTnews Awards. Additionally, he has programmed performances by artists like David Lamelas, Tanya Lukin Linklater, Will Rawls, and Wu Tsang.

He also organized two collection shows, “Endless” (in 2023) and “Interiors” (2022), and served as co-director of the MCA DNA Research Initiative, which produced new scholarship on the museum’s collection. He also was a member of the curatorial teams for Carla Acevedo-Yates’s two major group shows, “Dancing the Revolution: From Dancehall to Reggaetón” (2026) and “Forecast Form: Art in the Caribbean Diaspora, 1990s—Today” (2022).

Jimbo previously held curatorial positions at the Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art (MASS MoCA) and the Dallas Museum of Art. He contributed texts about several artists in the 2024 Whitney Biennial for the accompanying catalog.

“I look forward to building upon [the Whitney’s] legacy while advocating for emerging and overlooked artistic practices, particularly at this moment when the museum is attracting ever younger and more diverse audiences,” Jimbo said in a statement. “Relationships are at the heart of this work, and I am very excited to collaborate closely with artists as well as the Whitney’s vibrant community of colleagues and supporters.”

At the Whitney, Jimbo will organize and collaborate on exhibitions and public programs, as well as help grow the museum’s collection. “His appointment reflects the Whitney’s ongoing commitment to championing artists and expanding narratives of American art through exhibitions, collections, scholarship, and public engagement,” a release reads.

“Nolan is a star among a new generation of curators with fresh perspectives on art both past and present,” Whitney director Scott Rothkopf said in a statement. “His work moves fluidly between exhibitions, performance, and scholarship, and his expertise in Asian diasporic artists will add to new narratives in American art. We are thrilled to welcome him to the Whitney and look forward to the contributions he will make to our collection and program.”
excerpt_original: He is currently an assistant curator at the MCA Chicago.

article_text:
Vietnamese whodunit “ Karaoke Murder ” will open in cinemas across North America, Europe, Australia and Asia on the same weekend, a first for a film from Vietnam , according to its backers.

The film, titled “Án Mạng Karaoke” in Vietnamese, will bow nationwide at home on Oct. 30. U.S.-based specialty distributor 3388 Films will release it that same weekend in the U.S., Canada, the U.K., France, Germany, Norway, Australia and New Zealand, landing in time for Halloween. 3388 Films holds exclusive international rights in North America, Europe, Australia and New Zealand, Japan and Taiwan.

Related Stories

Netflix Q3 Revenue Meets Wall Street Estimates, Forecasts Q4 Slowdown and Says It Will Miss Ad Sales Target for the Year

'Beast in Me' Season 2 Casts John Goodman

“Karaoke Murder” is Hoang Le’s first film as director. Director-producer Vo Thanh Hoa of 89s Group serves as creative director, with Mai Bao Ngoc producing. 89s Group and F35 Studio are the production companies. The ensemble cast includes Doan Thien An, Thanh Son, Dai Nghia, Van Dung, Phuong Dung, Tieu Bao Ngoc, Tuyen Map, Quynh Ly, Ta Lam and Trinh Thao.

Set on a mountain pilgrimage taken by a group of neighbors, the film follows a former journalist who has to put her old investigative skills back to work after a widely loathed, karaoke-obsessed tycoon is killed overnight. With the group cut off from the outside world, suspicion falls on everyone.

Thien A. Pham, founder of 3388 Films, said the company had previously distributed titles on four continents as part of their international rollouts. “Aligning an international release with a film’s local date is a significant breakthrough moment. It’s what we’ve advocated for years because we believe greater momentum can be generated for international films when local and international release dates sync up,” Pham said. “It’s energizing to have gutsy partners, like the producers of ‘Karaoke Murder,’ as 3388 Films continues to redefine possibilities for Asian films.”

The producers said they built the story around karaoke because of the place it holds in Vietnamese life. Singing sessions are part of weddings, birthdays and Lunar New Year, as well as ordinary Sunday afternoons, and nearly every household owns a speaker and microphone. The pastime also causes friction. Vietnam penalizes noise after 10 p.m., karaoke ranks among the most common causes of rows between neighbors and news outlets report karaoke disputes ending in tragedy every year, according to the producers.

“We’re proud – but above all, grateful,” said Vo. “For years, our belief has been simple: ‘win at home first – then travel with your own voice.’ We make films for Vietnamese audiences before anyone else.”

Vo said 89s Group’s films had grossed more than VND600 billion ($23 million) at the Vietnamese box office between 2023 and 2026. “That foundation gives us the confidence to step onto the world stage – not by imitating others, but with our own voice,” Vo said. “I hope the Vietnamese diaspora will feel a little piece of home when they watch ‘Karaoke Murder.’ And I hope international audiences leave the theater a little more curious about Vietnamese cinema – and perhaps a little more careful the next time they pick up a microphone.”

3388 Films has specialized in Asian content for more than 20 years. Its recent releases include “Mai,” the first Vietnamese film to cross $2 million at the North American and European box office.

article_text:
Painel durante a D23 também indicou possíveis participações de Hugh Jackman e Ryan Reynolds como Wolverine e Deadpool, respectivamente.

Durante seu painel na conferência D23, a Marvel divulgou um novo trailer de “ Vingadores: Doutor Destino “. O vilão vivido por Robert Downey Jr. é confrontado por todos os heróis, incluindo Vingadores, Quarteto Fantástico e X-Men. Assista acima (legendado).

Assista abaixo à versão dublada.

Foi divulgado também um novo cartaz internacional, abaixo.

Até o momento, estão confirmados nomes como Robert Downey Jr. como o vilão Victor von Doom/Doutor Destino e nomes de diversos outros cantos do MCU, como “Quarteto Fantástico”, “Thunderbolts*”, “Capitão América: Admirável Mundo Novo”, e até mesmo os antigos filmes da franquia “X-Men” da Fox nos anos 2000 — veja a lista completa .

Durante o painel na D23, um vídeo com Hugh Jackman e Ryan Reynolds também deu a entender que a dupla — intérpretes de Wolverine e Deadpool, respectivamente — também pode aparecer no filme. Com Reynolds sussurrando as falas ao fundo, Jacksman diz querer “apenas dar um alô, sem nenhum aviso prévio” para saber se Kevin Feige, o chefão da Marvel nos cinemas, “precisaria de ajuda para completar o elenco.” Jackman completa afirmando que talvez até consiga “convencer Ryan [Reynolds] a aparecer em ‘Vingadores: Doutor Destino’.”

“Doutor Destino” e sua sequência, “Vingadores: Guerras Secretas”, terão direção dos irmãos Joe e Anthony Russo, que já dirigiram outros quatro filmes do MCU, incluindo “Vingadores: Guerra Infinita” e “Ultimato”. O roteiro é de Stephen McFeely, que também trabalhou com os irmãos Russo nos filmes anteriores.

“Vingadores: Doutor Destino” tem estreia prevista para 17 de dezembro de 2026.

article_text:
For more than a century, a suite of murals by Symbolist painter Odilon Redon have decorated the library of the Abbaye de Fontfroide, an 11th-century former monastery in the South of France. When they were removed earlier this year for the first time since their installation to be loaned for a high-profile exhibition, a set of test drawings, until then unknown, by Redon were uncovered.

“It was a great surprise—nobody imagined the existence of these sketches,” Alexandre d’Andoque de Sériège, Abbaye de Fontfroide’s director, told ARTnews in an interview. “It amuses just to imagine Redon painting them on the wall.”

Installed upon their completion in 1911, the three paneled works— Le Jour (Day), La Nuit (Night), and Le Silence (Silence)—were commissioned by Gustave Fayet . Fayet was one of the turn of century’s great French collectors, but he is now little-known. The breadth of Fayet’s holdings is now coming into view via a blockbuster exhibition , “Gustave Fayet, Collector-Designer: Icons of Modern Art,” at the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris, which has gathered around 250 works of the 750 works that once passed through his hands.

The drawings’ discovery was even more surprising because neither Fayet nor Redon had ever written about their existence, either in correspondence to each other or to other members of the French avant-garde. It’s possible that they might have been an initial test for a fresco, but “a fresco in the library would have required Redon to stay very long in Fontfroide. It’s also physically a very hard job,” d’Andoque de Sériège, who is also Fayet’s grandson, said. “So, I think it’s really just a painting for fun.”

That theory is supported by the fact that the newly discovered wall drawings don’t resemble the final works, which were begun in Redon’s Paris studio. “The figures are more colorful [on the wall] than the figures in panels. The shape is typical Redon, but not the choice of colors,” d’Andoque de Sériège said. “The two female figures—Madeleine and Simone [his wife and daughter]—are very tall, very important in the panels, but in the sketches on the walls they are rather small, only 30–35 centimeters high.”

Fayet met Redon in 1900 and purchased his first work by the artist the following year; he eventually came to own some 300 works of his. Fayet would visit Redon each time he took the train up to Paris, and they grew closer still when the collector’s family moved to Paris in 1905. The friendship also influenced Fayet as a painter: He started out making Realist pictures in the style of the Barbizon School before taking up the Impressionist style. When he met Redon, Fayet “moved to a sort of emotional painting, and I think that’s why he bought so many paintings from Redon and the Nabis,” d’Andoque de Sériège said.

Fayet’s purchase of Fontfroide slowed down his collecting, which began in 1899, the year he took over the family business and purchased 41 works from the collection of Armand Carbol, another winemaker from Béziers. His decision to buy the abbey was one that came of familiarity. The Domaine de Vedilhan, one of the Fayet’s family vineyards near Narbonne, is about 12 miles northeast of the Abbaye de Fontfroide.

“Fayet’s family knew Fontfroide for a long time before Fayet himself bought it in 1908,” d’Andoque de Sériège said. “His father, Gabriel, was a painter [who] painted the cloister of Fontfroide and the portrait of the last abbot of Fontfroide,” whom the Fayet visited in 1895 with Madeline.

But Fayet also wanted to prevent Fontfroide’s destruction. After the 1901 Law of Associations, which suppressed religious orders and seized their properties, many historical religious sites were bought so their masonry could be repurposed to make new buildings, according to d’Andoque de Sériège. (Fayet was first outbid in his quest to buy Fontfroide, which had already been sold twice, but he offered 10 percent more, triggering an auction, where he paid 49,925 francs to buy it in January 1908.)

“[Fayet] intended to turn his property into a vibrant, creative place, imbued with a fully Symbolist philosophy in which great pagan myths could enter into dialogue with Christian sensibilities in a natural setting steeped in a sacred tradition,” d’Andoque de Sériège writes in an essay he coauthored with art historian Pierre Pinchon on Redon’s decoration for Fontfroide. “Fayet’s intentions naturally appealed to Redon, who had recently been steering his work toward a pantheistic celebration of nature and a glorification of the solar myths through Apollonian, Orphic, and floral subjects.”

Redon first visited Fontfroide in October 1908, and when he arrived, he immediately noticed the statue of Diana and Apollo that Fayet had installed near the entrance. That would ultimately impact the design for Le Jour . When Redon returned in March 1910 for a 10-day stay, the restoration of the library had been completed, and he had a better sense of how his commission would sit in the space.

“At that period, they discussed the project because it was easier to see room, the importance of the wall, to look at the light through the windows,” d’Andoque de Sériège said. “We guess—we are 99 percent sure—that it is during that that stay that Redon made the sketches we discovered when we removed the panels.”

While Redon made decorative panels for other sites in France, the panels at Fontfroide are the only ones that still remain in situ in their original location, according to d’Andoque de Sériège. As their titles indicate, the two larger works, Le Jour and La Nuit , are in dialogue with each other.

“The two decorative panels are a testament to the whole career of Redon,” he said. “ La Nuit is an echo of the ‘Noirs’ period of Redon, and Le Jour echoes the second period of Redon, with the theme of Apollo and Diana, but more generally with all the flowers, the bouquets, and the use of color.”

He continued, “The second reason for the importance of this decoration is it reflects finally the taste of Gustave Fayet, who first collected the ‘Noirs’ and then moved to the flowers and mythological themes of Redon. Fayet also sold [parts of his collection] in 1910, just a few months before, so it’s a period where he is reorganizing his collection around Gauguin, van Gogh, Redon, and others.”

After the Fondation Louis Vuitton exhibition, the Redon works will return to Fontfroide, as their installation was classified a few years ago by the French state as a historical monument, joining the cloister, abbey, and chapter house which were designated as such in the 19th century. Fontfroide had to receive a special authorization from the Ministry of Culture in order to loan them to the exhibition.

“It is the first and only time we will do that,” d’Andoque de Sériège said. “Very few people have heard of Fayet. The exhibition at Fondation Louis Vuittion will shed light on Fayet, but it will be visible only during five months in Paris. After the exhibition, the only thing you can see from Fayet is Fontfroide, and what he did for the restoration: the sculpture, the gardens, the tiles, the library, everything. We have to be much more precise and say much more about Fayet at Fontfroide because today when you visit Fontfroide, we say very little about Fayet, which was a mistake from my family.”

article_text:
A high-speed traffic accident leaves a college student in a wheelchair for life, but that’s merely the starting point of the narrative in “ To Be Ordinary ,” a sensitive, slowly enveloping film with scant interest in disability-drama cliché — instead offering an expansive portrait of how the young man’s entire family is affected by his accident over the course of more than a decade. Spanning marital strife, economic upheaval, coming-of-age pains and moral crisis, Taiwanese writer-director Lee Yun Chan ‘s fourth feature — her first since 2010’s “Dancing Without You” — has a lot of story to wrangle, but does so with a mostly delicate, empathetic touch, with a script that treats all individuals in this unhappy scenario with equal care and interest.

Related Stories

'Nick Cannon @ Night' Podcast Moves to BET, Will Relaunch as a Weekly TV Talk Show (EXCLUSIVE)

Since her last film, Lee has done mostly small-screen work — directing, among other things, the 2022 Disney+ series “Women in Taipei” — and if a certain televisual strain of melodrama occasional creeps into “To Be Ordinary,” the film’s sturdy formal restraint and expansive story scope should still serve it well in cinemas. Following its premiere as the only Taiwanese production in Busan’s main competition, the film will play at the Tokyo Film Festival later this month, opening theatrically in Taiwan in mid-November. Further festival play is likely, particularly in Asian-focused programs, and the film is accessible and moving enough for limited global distribution, though specialist streaming platforms may be its best bet.

Lee, who co-wrote the screenplay with “Women in Taipei” scribe Ginger Wang, wastes little time setting the story into motion, opening on a lovely, gliding nighttime tracking shot of 22-year-old Yu-jie (Junior Hsieh) on his moped, cruising the rain-slicked roads of suburban Taipei, as the grandiose strings of Cicada’s score conjure a false feeling of serenity. DP Ming Lee’s camera will certainly never be this free again; the reverie stops short when, at an intersection, Yu-jie is struck by a car, driven by the wealthy, elderly Mr Ma (Hsiu Shen Liang), who’s immediately beset with irremediable guilt.

Yu-jie survives the accident but soon learns, in hospital, that he’ll never walk again; a college student who has already started his own web design business, he accepts the bad news with remarkable stoicism, quickly adapting to life in a wheelchair and seeking ways to live the most normal, productive life possible — which includes a budding relationship with young hospital physiotherapist Yi-Han (Phoebe Chu).

If anything, the rest of his family has a harder time adjusting. His mother (Chang Shih Ying) and father (Weber Yang) were already at a fraught point in their marriage, and their son’s plight only drives them further apart, the situation exacerbated by Dad’s longtime unemployment. Meanwhile, Yu-jie’s younger sister Yu-ching (Pin Hsuan Chen), already facing the hormonal turmoil of early adolescence, feels sidelined by the tragedy — pressured to look after herself while, as her mother puts it, “there’s enough going on at home” — and begins to lash out.

At a pragmatic level, the family is aided by Mr Ma’s crushing conscience: In addition to the required legal settlement, he transfers ownership of his entire house to Yu-jie, and continues to contribute generously toward his medical bills and living expenses. But such generosity can itself become a burden of sorts to the benefactor, particularly as Mr Ma retreats into old age and ill health; avoiding drawing its characters along victims-and-villains lines, “To Be Ordinary” reserves compassion for all in this wretched turn of events, which gives it welcome dramatic complexity and maturity, particularly as the story spans 11 years of evolving consequences.

Thoughtful, closely-knit ensemble playing keeps the family dynamic believable even when the script takes a few convenient short cuts: Chen is especially affecting and volatile as a young woman growing up both as a kind of afterthought, and as a support system to her flailing parents. Lee directs proceedings with a handsome sobriety that befits the material, though between the persistently overcast visuals and the solemnly emotive writing, “To Be Ordinary” could stand an occasional injection of tonal surprise — an acknowledgement of the absurdity, hilarity or small domestic joys that sometimes disrupt hard times. Still, the film is never glib or unconsidered. There’s unassuming beauty in its even-handed, fair-minded worldview, and the space it gives its characters to reckon with sorrow, and find their own way out of it.

‘To Be Ordinary’ Review: A Compassionate, Even-Handed Taiwanese Family Melodrama

Reviewed at Busan Film Festival (Competition), Oct. 13, 2026. Running time: 112 MIN.

Crew: Director: Lee Yun Chan. Screenplay: Lee, Ginger Wang. Camera: Ming Lee. Editor: Su Ling Tu. Music: Cicada.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Xochitl Gomez , Madeleine McGraw and Jack Champion are hitting the road for the Jason Perlman-helmed YA horror film Bad Influence .

The trio has been cast in the film from screenwriter Brandon Cohen, which is described as a modern-day Thelma & Louise fueled by female rage, following Isabelle (McGraw) and Kira (Gomez) on a road trip home for spring break, when they pick up mysterious hitchhiker (Liam), who is not what he seems.

Bad Influence producers are Debbie Liebling, Joel David Moore and Zachary Burgess. Moore and Liebling previously collaborated on Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story (2004) and Grandma’s Boy (2006). Executive producers include Steven Silverstein, Cathy Raduns, Raymond Merrill, Carmelo Chimera, Syed Ali Saeed, Denis Schoenhofer, Natalie Kline, Jarod Einsohn and Michelle and Melissa Macedo.

Related Stories

Xochitl Gomez Joins CBS’s ‘Boston Blue’ Cast As Recurring Guest Star

Jack Champion Joins Netflix Comedy ‘Don’t Say Good Luck’

Gomez is known for her roles in Marvel’s Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness , Netflix’s The Babysitters Club and Season 32 of ABC’s Dancing with the Stars , which she won. She can next be heard in the Warner Bros’ animated update on Dr. Seuss’ The Cat in the Hat . Gomez is repped by Savage Agency, Rain and Myman Greenspan.

Watch on Deadline

McGraw reprised her role as Gwen Blake in The Black Phone 2 , having also appeared in American Sniper , Cars 3 , Ant-Man and the Wasp and Toy Story 4 . She is repped by UTA, The Burstein Company, Coast to Coast Talent Group and Schreck Rose.

Champion has starred as Spider in the Avatar franchise, in addition to appearing in Scream VI . His latest movie Don’t Say Good Luck recently premiered on Netflix. Champion is repped by UTA, Amplified and Goodman Genow.

Capture is handling sales on the Bad Influence .

"translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这也让关于奥斯卡的讨论变得合情合理。赛义夫里德在《无所遁形》中展现了极其真实而赤诚的一面——而且并非无关紧要的是，她贡献了影片后半部分最令人难忘的幽默。（她对埃文斯控制霍姆斯形象及生活的方式日益感到震惊，当霍姆斯本人退场后，这为观众继续投入故事提供了一个引人入胜的切入点。）但无论她能否在某种程度上打破常规——尽管有着类似的前例（2020年《波拉特》续集中的玛丽亚·巴卡洛娃曾因在现实生活中的即兴反应而获得提名），但这几乎是一个前所未例的案例——赛义夫里德所做的事情比赢得任何奖项都更为令人印象深刻。她将自己作为演员的工作——包括她的准备过程，以及饰演一个健在之人的道德问题——置于仔细审视之下，并表现出足够的脆弱，试图将这一切剖析清楚，同时也展露出她内心的不确定。这种出场、表演，或无论称之为什么的形式，都将在奥斯卡季之后被久久讨论。它将赛义夫里德定位在我们早就该认识到的样子：她属于她那一代人中最具胆识的明星之列。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “ You Can See Everything ,” now playing in theaters.

The question that’s consumed the awards-pundit class since “You Can See Everything” exploded into theaters last week is whether Amanda Seyfried , the unlikely linchpin of this hybrid documentary, can be nominated for or win an acting Oscar. A24 is planning to campaign her for one. Much of her time onscreen is as herself, reacting in real time — but she does, eventually, re-enact co-director Nathan Fielder’s remembered interactions with disgraced tech founder Elizabeth Holmes .

New York's AMC Kips Bay Theater Closes on Jan. 3; CEO Says 'AMC Wants to Stay' but NYU Langone 'Wants Us Gone'

In this, she’s reprising a role that, with the 2022 Hulu series “The Dropout,” already won her an Emmy and a Golden Globe. It’s the role, now that “You Can See Everything” is on track to become one of the most financially successful documentaries in history, that’s become Seyfried’s signature. To this viewer, the question is at once an amusing thought experiment ( sure, why not? ), and a testament to Seyfried’s compelling screen presence — and more than a little beside the point. For once, an Oscar seems minimizing. What Seyfried’s doing in her most compelling screen work ever is something other, or more, than simply acting.

Popular on Variety

To be clear, the parts of “You Can See Everything” when she is literally acting are riveting on their own terms. Seyfried simply wears the role of Holmes easily. She’s doubly disadvantaged — in that we’ve just spent 90 minutes with the real Holmes, against whom we can compare Seyfried, and in that we’ve also spent time absorbing just how little Seyfried understands the enigma of Holmes’ motivations. And yet Seyfried somehow creates a coherent and compelling version of a woman we don’t understand, and we know she doesn’t, really, either.

To pigeonhole Seyfried’s appearance in “You Can See Everything” as, solely, an acting performance misses the rawness of Seyfried’s presence here. She allows herself to be seen thinking through a conundrum, as herself, and falling short of finding answers — in other words, after Holmes and husband Billy Evans, she’s the documentary’s other subject. Seyfried delivers a painful and unresolved excavation of the mind of an actor, seeming to land in a place of uncertainty as to how her own past work as Holmes has changed the story even as she willingly takes on the part once more.

Consider, for instance, the scene in which Seyfried visits Evans at home, after Holmes’ incarceration. This is impressively game and daring. And Seyfried is, I suppose, “acting,” both in the theorist’s sense that all of us are acting our way through life and in the particular that Seyfried has set out to lure information out of Evans to better understand the seemingly bizarre arrangement Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim had been excavating before Holmes went to prison. But is she acting, in the traditional sense, when she meets and interacts with Holmes and Evans’ two children, or when she defends her social media post criticizing the late Charlie Kirk against Evans’ mockery? Alternately tender and outraged, Seyfried allows us into her world, just as Holmes tried to. But Holmes, talking past real questioning, couldn’t get there, no matter how all-access her invitation to Fielder had been. Seyfried, by contrast, seems deeply in touch with emotions lying just under the surface. And her increasing befuddlement both matches our own and raises the question of just how deeply an actor can ever understand their subject.

Seyfried, just as Holmes and Evans do in their askew manner, knows her angles. It wasn’t lost on me that within the frame as Fielder speaks to her at her home is a miniature playhouse, of the sort her company Make It Cute sells. That the computer on which she and Fielder watch video of Holmes watching “The Dropout” is propped on coffee table books about Seyfried’s great passion, dogs, and that she and Fielder discuss Holmes while feeding her photogenic horses on her photogenic farm only burnish her brand further. And yet she cannot help but exposing more than she may mean to.

A conversation about the ethics of “The Dropout” — a drama based on real events that, as with any dramatization, used creative license, and that many viewers took as fact — places Seyfried in a surprisingly exposed position. Holmes did not, literally, say and do all the things that Seyfried says and does in the role, Seyfried admits, but she may well have, and the performance overall conjures the sense of a person who is unconcerned with scientific accuracy or with the truth. Shouldn’t that be enough? “I didn’t do that to her,” Seyfried concludes, after attempting to walk herself through a justification of “The Dropout” as plainly not depicting objective reality, no matter what viewers think. “She did that to herself.” She seems to be convincing herself not to feel guilty, up until her final line, delivered with a “It’s Chinatown”-style futility. “It’s very complicated,” she says, having indulged the complications long enough.

Coming into “You Can See Everything,” this viewer saw Elizabeth Holmes’ Theranos as transparently fraudulent and “The Dropout” as an excellent TV show that was in no need of moral justification. Leaving the theater, nothing about those beliefs had changed, but engaging the question of what Seyfried might have owed to Holmes allowed both women to be seen in intriguing new lights. Seyfried, painfully aware of the existence of the two young children she’d met, twists around the question of whether her past work might have been unfair, or have been presented as possessed of a truth its creators didn’t actually know. And in this moment, she seems less to be acting than to be, in a moment of painful frankness I admire her for allowing herself to experience on-camera, acted upon.

Say this much: “You Can See Everything” is undeniably a career high for an actor who has seemed at times in her career like an underdog. (A sliding-doors scenario for the ages: The role of Elizabeth Holmes originally went to sketch comedian Kate McKinnon, and Seyfried got the role only after McKinnon dropped out and Seyfried got a career-boosting Oscar nomination for 2020’s “Mank.”) Amiably loopy in interviews — including in red-carpet appearances at this year’s Academy Museum Gala, where Seyfried sidestepped discussing the film in favor of free-associative Dada — and impressively shifting between genres to avoid being pigeonholed, Seyfried is easy to root for, but can seem hard to know.

Which makes the Oscar talk make perfect sense. Seyfried has gone to a very raw place in “You Can See Everything” — and, not for nothing, has delivered some of the most memorable humor in its second half. (Her growing scandalization at Evans’ control over Holmes’ image and her life allows the viewer a compelling way to stay engaged with the story once Holmes herself leaves it.) But whether or not she can break through in what would, despite vaguely similar precedent — Maria Bakalova in the 2020 “Borat” sequel was nominated for reacting against real life — be close to an unprecedented case, Seyfried has done something more impressive than earning any award. She’s opened up her work as an actor — both her preparation and the moral question of what it means to play a living person — to careful scrutiny, and was vulnerable enough to attempt to talk it through, and to be shown to be uncertain. This appearance, or performance, or whatever, will be discussed far beyond Oscar season. It situates Seyfried as what we ought to have known she was all along: Among the most daring stars of her generation.

article_text:
The 9th edition of El Gouna Film Festival (Oct. 15-23) may be celebrating Mona Zaki ’s past, but the Egyptian film star is far more interested in what she’s yet to do.

Honored with the festival’s Career Achievement Award at the opening ceremony, Zaki, who has already built a career spanning more than three decades, hasn’t even turned 50. Sitting down with Variety on the shores of the Red Sea, she speaks about that prolific career less as a completed body of work than a continuous process of reinvention. That ongoing transformation has required her to repeatedly shed audiences’ expectations of who Mona Zaki should be. “I get bored easily with myself,” she shares.

Related Stories

Hulu's Mother-Son Mystery 'Phony' Mutes Connie Britton's Charisma Under Visual Effects: TV Review

Looking back, Zaki says two lessons in particular stand out: learning the power of saying “no” and finding the confidence and willingness to express herself, both personally and emotionally. The latter, she confides, was something acting itself helped teach her.

Popular on Variety

“You just have to open up,” she reflects. “Your emotions are important to be heard, and it’s okay. Part of your healing is saying what you feel.”

Zaki entered the industry young, first in theater, before moving into television and, ultimately, the silver screen. Early on, she became closely associated with the “girl next door,” an image that increasingly felt at odds with both the woman she was becoming and the kinds of characters she wanted to explore.

“I started to kind of feel like I’m going there doing the same thing in every different project,” she recalls. “How boring is that? I needed to shift.”

That turning point came with Yousry Nasrallah’s 2009 drama “ Scheherazade, Tell Me a Story ” (Ehky Ya Shahrazad), written by the late Wahid Hamed, which saw Zaki take on the role of a television host whose program examines the experiences of women navigating romance, health, everyday life, and the expectations placed upon them by Egyptian society.

The departure from Zaki’s familiar screen persona drew intense backlash, with audiences questioning what had happened to the “girl next door” they had come to know. The response shook her enough that she turned to Hamed with concerns about facing the film’s promotional tour. He encouraged her to stand behind a choice she had made out of love for the work, advice that helped Zaki confront the resistance to seeing her move beyond the roles that had defined her early career.

For Zaki, the experience marked the beginning of a struggle that has followed her throughout her career, that of finding roles that allow women to address subjects Egyptian cinema has historically treated as difficult or off-limits. “Censorship, talking about taboos, things that are not okay most of the time, especially for women to talk about,” remain among the challenges she continues to face. “I’m still living in that struggle even now. It can be very difficult to find a meaningful script.”

While she believes the landscape has advanced over more than 30 years, Zaki remains deeply frustrated by the gap between the talent of Egypt’s actresses and the opportunities afforded them. “It breaks my heart that most of them are not taking the chances they deserve and the topics they would love to talk about and the rights they want to stand for.”

Her own connection with audiences is something she has learned to negotiate over time. “It’s a relationship. You work on it like any other relationship in your life,” she explains. Part of that relationship, she believes, means establishing boundaries around her freedom to evolve as an artist.

“I have the right not to feel bored and sick of myself doing the same thing because I’m not corporate, I’m an artist,” she stresses. “Art is about freedom, it’s about change, it’s about trial and error.”

With each role, Zaki starts by building a life for the character beyond what exists in the script. She works with an acting coach on every project, drawing on different techniques to construct the character’s history.

One of the most important parts of that process, she explains, is imagining a character’s life before the audience ever meets her. Zaki might close her eyes and picture the woman she’s playing at seven years old, in her childhood home with her mother, building memories and emotional associations that will never appear on screen but are critical to the performance. “I don’t have to say it, but I can make people feel it the way I felt it.”

That method was put to a different test with “ El Sett ,” Marwan Hamed’s biopic of Umm Kulthum. This time, Zaki was building a character from the life of one of the Arab world’s most revered cultural figures, with decades of history and public memory with which to contend. She plunged into what she calls “crazy research,” watching every piece of footage she could find and repeatedly listening to a rare two-hour radio interview that became one of her most important references.

“The whole internal emotions are the imagination of the writer and me.” While the facts of Umm Kulthum’s life are immutable, Zaki still had to find the woman behind them.

To bridge that gap, Zaki imagined the parts of Kulthum’s life no archive could relate: the emotions, relationships and private struggles that might have shaped her from childhood. The character stayed with Zaki long after cameras stopped rolling, and she found it difficult to sever that connection after filming wrapped.

“I came out of the project feeling that I’m a 70-year-old woman. I’m serious, this was not a joke.” For months, she had taken on not only the physical transformation into Kulthum, but also the emotions and experiences of a woman decades older than herself. Fully returning to Mona Zaki proved disorienting. “I think my whole face changed after that,” she recalls. “I couldn’t accept myself in the mirror.”

Some of Kulthum has proven difficult to shake. “I’m trying to get rid of her,” Zaki muses. “I only have a few leftovers, gladly. Honestly, I don’t want to feel like I’m 70 and I’m not there yet.”

Asked what she looks for in a role now, after more than three decades of acting, Zaki doesn’t hesitate. “Reality. Honesty. That would just take my heart.”

I would just like to mention a few films with which I engaged in a deep, personal, and meaningful way this year. What strikes me about the list is that the works come from everywhere, including places where I’ve found it very difficult to find anything cinematically powerful lately: big-budget productions, blockbusters, films with a long list of labs in the opening credits, and works made by the usual suspects of the Cannes Film Festival. It’s exciting to notice that under all those logos, there’s still cinema breathing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I don’t believe in the usual hierarchy between formats, so I wanted to name ten The results are in for our 2025 poll of Film Comment ’s contributors and colleagues! On this page you’ll find a selection of the individual ballots submitted by our voters for the Best Films of 2025 category, covering features that were released either theatrically or virtually in 2025 in the United States. To see which films came out on top, check out our Best Films of 2025 list, which features original appreciations from critics, as well as links to features, reviews, and interviews about these films and directors from across the year.

Don’t see your favorite? Check out our Best Undistributed Films of 2025 list, featuring films that premiered this year but have not yet announced stateside distribution. And don’t miss our Best of 2025 Countdown Podcast , featuring guest critics Amy Taubin and Bilge Ebiri.

Also available in the links above: critic and programmer Inney Prakash’s list of the year’s Best Short Films , filmmaker and programmer Gina Telaroli’s list of the Best Restorations , critic and editor Gavin Smith’s list of the year’s Best Repertory Releases , and writing on the Best Scenes by Devika Girish ands the Best Performances by Michael Koresky.

The Ballad of Suzanne Césaire

The order for me is not very important. I would just like to mention a few films with which I engaged in a deep, personal, and meaningful way this year. What strikes me about the list is that the works come from everywhere, including places where I’ve found it very difficult to find anything cinematically powerful lately: big-budget productions, blockbusters, films with a long list of labs in the opening credits, and works made by the usual suspects of the Cannes Film Festival. It’s exciting to notice that under all those logos, there’s still cinema breathing.

I don’t believe in the usual hierarchy between formats, so I wanted to name ten short and medium-length films that were as (or even more) important than the aforementioned features for me this year: Breu Febril (Wallace Douglas), Filme Sem Querer (Lincoln Péricles), Feiura Comovente (Ultra Martini), Piel de Toro Muerto (Aroldo Murguia), Abajo y a la Izquierda (Martín Baus), The Goblin Play (Chae Yu), Revolving Rounds (Johann Lurf, Christina Jauernik), Daimara y el Baile Zombie (Natalia Keiko, Tom Hamburguer), Bounded Intimacy (Ayanna Dozier).

"这一表述似乎已化为现实。10月30日，香港的M+、纽约现代艺术博物馆（MoMA）以及巴黎的蓬皮杜艺术中心宣布建立前所未有规模的全面文化伙伴关系。该合作的核心内容是一项协议：将三馆的藏品视为一个共享的藏品库，由横跨三个大洲的工作人员共同策划。", "links": [{"text": "香港", "url": "https://artnewsjapan.com/tag/hong_kong"}, Cherix）共同接受的联合采访中表示：“如果这一尝试成功，我们将不仅是三家博物馆的简单相加，而是能够成为超越这个总和的存在。这是一项非常崭新的举措。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "共享收藏规模达数十万件", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "仅将MoMA和蓬皮杜中心的藏品合并，共享收藏的总数就已达到数十万件。此外，三家博物馆都管理着庞大的档案。开馆6年的M+拥有约8,000件藏品，以瑞士实业家、前外交官乌里·希格（Uli Sigg）捐赠的作品为核心，堪称中国当代艺术收藏的典范。另一方面，拥有欧洲最大现代艺术博物馆的蓬皮杜中心，其藏品则属于法国政府所有的国家级收藏。", "translated": true}, {"type": "在巴黎的采访中，3位馆长承认此次合作建立在以往2馆间伙伴关系的基础之上，但他们同时强调，这是从3馆共同的理念与历史谱系中孕育而生的。这不仅指它们在跨门类的收藏方针以及对当代艺术的关注上具有共同点，也指向从1929年MoMA成立到1977年蓬皮杜艺术中心开馆，再到2021年M+开馆，延续了大约1个世纪的现代美术收藏谱系。拉费尔也回顾称，在亚洲建立M+这样的美术馆时，蓬皮杜艺术中心正是作为理念指南而参考的主要机构之一。", "近年来，旨在实现藏品共享、资源汇聚以及扩大观众群体的美术馆合作日益增多。其形式也从传统的短期作品借贷，演变为共同购买、个人联合捐赠、构建区域网络以及长期的国际交流等更具深度的模式。自2003年惠特尼美术馆、泰特美术馆和蓬皮杜艺术中心3馆共同收藏比尔·维奥拉（Bill Viola）的影像装置作品《Five Angels for the Millennium》以来，共同购买变得越来越普遍。", MoMA、ポンピドゥー・センター、M+が異例の提携を発表。3館の所蔵品を単一のコレクションとして共有へ

ニューヨーク近代美術館（MoMA）、パリのポンピドゥー・センター、香港のM+が、前例のない規模の包括的な提携を発表した。3館の所蔵品をひとつの共有コレクションとして扱い、3大陸のスタッフが共同でキュレーションを行うという。持続可能な運営を目指し、従来の枠組みを超えて美術館の新しい未来を描く試みだ。

6年前、香港の美術館 M+ の館長スハンヤ・ラフェルは、文化戦略家アンドラス・サントの著書『The Future of the Museum（美術館の未来）』のインタビューで、今後の美術館は「より持続可能な運営基盤を築くため、連帯して助け合う必要がある」と語った。さらに、美術館の次なる章ではコラボレーションが重要な鍵になるとも。

その言葉は現実のものとなったようだ。10月30日、 香港 のM+、 ニューヨーク近代美術館（MoMA） 、 パリ の ポンピドゥー・センター は、前例のない規模の包括的な文化提携を発表した。提携の核となるのは、3館の所蔵品をひとつの共有コレクションとして扱い、3大陸にまたがるスタッフがキュレーションを手がけるという合意だ。

ポンピドゥー・センターの館長であるローラン・ル・ボンは、M+のラフェルやMoMAの館長であるクリストフ・シェリックスとともにパリで応じた合同インタビューで、「この試みが成功すれば、単に3館を足し合わせた以上の存在になれるでしょう。これは非常に新しい取り組みです」と語った。

共有コレクションは数十万点規模

MoMAとポンピドゥー・センターの所蔵品を合わせるだけでも、共有コレクションの総数は数十万点にのぼる。さらに3館はいずれも膨大なアーカイブを管理している。6年前に開館したM+の所蔵品は約8,000点だが、スイスの実業家で元外交官のウリ・シグから寄贈された作品を軸に、中国現代美術の決定版ともいえるコレクションを誇る。一方、ヨーロッパ最大の近代美術館を擁するポンピドゥー・センターの所蔵品は、フランス政府が所有する国立コレクションだ。

見込まれる観客層の規模も計り知れない。現在の数値に基づけば、3館の合計で年間1,000万人の来館者と、1億2,500万人のオンライン訪問者にリーチできることになる。

長期貸与や企画展など順次始動

コレクションの共有は、複数のプロジェクトから順次始動する。2027年後半には、M+の主要作品が長期貸与のかたちでMoMAのコレクション・ギャラリーに展示されるほか、2028年にはMoMA館内にポンピドゥー・センターの長期展示室が開設される予定だ。同様の計画は他の2館でも並行して進められている（なお、ポンピドゥー・センターは現在5年間の大規模改修のため休館中で、2030年に再開予定だ）。

また提携の一環として、今後5年間にわたり「コンテンポラリー」という複雑な概念を探求する共同企画展も開催される。3館すべての所蔵品で構成され、各館を巡回する予定だ。さらに、北米や西欧以外の美術史を調査するためMoMAが2009年に立ち上げた部門横断型のリサーチプログラム、C-MAP（Contemporary and Modern Art Perspectives）に、ポンピドゥー・センターとM+のキュレーターが参加することも決まっている。

このほか、3館の館長や部門長、キュレーターで構成される合同運営委員会が発足し、展覧会やコレクションの共有、調査研究、修復・保存、専門人材の育成といった優先課題に取り組む。委員会は毎月会合を開くほか、年に1度は対面での大規模な年次会議を実施する。初回の年次会議は来月MoMAで行われ、以降は各館の持ち回りで開催される。

今回の提携は、M+と他の2館がこれまで個別に築いてきた協力関係を発展させたものでもある。2025年2月、M+とMoMAはコレクションの共有や共同研究、キュレーターの交流を盛り込んだ覚書を 締結した 。また今年初めには、M+とポンピドゥー・センターが複数年にわたる戦略的パートナーシップを 発表し 、ポンピドゥー・センターのリニューアルオープン記念展を両館の所蔵品で開催したのち、同展をM+へ巡回させる計画を明らかにしていた。

約1世紀にわたる現代美術の系譜

パリでのインタビューで3人の館長は、今回の提携がこれまでの2館間でのパートナーシップを土台にしていることを認めつつも、3館に共通する理念や歴史的系譜から生まれたものだと強調した。これはジャンルを横断する収集方針や同時代のアートへの注力といった共通点に加え、1929年のMoMA設立から1977年のポンピドゥー・センター開館、そして2021年のM+開館へと続く、約1世紀にわたる現代美術コレクションの系譜を指す。ラフェルも、アジアにM+のような美術館を設立するにあたり、理念の指針として参考にした主要な機関のひとつがポンピドゥー・センターだったと振り返る。

シェリックスは「それぞれの館が、世界にふたつとない独自のコレクションを持っている」としたうえで、「私たちの第一の使命はもちろん作品の保存です。しかし、それらのコレクションをさらに生かし、美術館の壁を越えてより多くの人々に届けるにはどうすればよいかを考えなければなりません」と語る。

収集から共有へ

さらにシェリックスは、今回の提携は巡回展や共同企画展、個別プロジェクトでの協業といった従来のモデルとは一線を画すものだと説明する。チーム同士の連携をこれまで以上に深め、ゼロから共にプログラムを作り上げていく長期的なコミットメントだからだ。

この新たな枠組みには、規模の経済を生かし、作品輸送などの環境負荷を抑えてより持続可能な運営を実現する狙いもある。ラフェルとシェリックスが例として挙げたのが、M+の中国現代美術コレクションのMoMAへの長期貸与だ。これにより、MoMAの展示室で作品を入れ替えながら公開できるだけでなく、米国内の他の美術館への貸し出しも容易になるという。

各美術館がグローバルな視点をコレクションに反映させようとする現在、個別に作品を買い集め続けるよりも、共有するほうが理にかなっている。「ただ収集し続けるわけにはいかないからこそ、私たちは共有を選んだのです」とラフェルは言う。結果として、新規収蔵のハードルはこれまで以上に高くなる。シェリックスの言葉を借りれば、今後共有コレクションに加わる作品は、3館のどこにも類を見ないものでなければならないからだ。

「どれほど同時代のアートに注力しようとしても、美術館の所蔵品はいずれ歴史的なコレクションになっていきます」とシェリックスは続ける。「それをどうリセットするか。今回の提携によって、これまでとは異なる視野と未来を見据えたビジョンを持つことが可能になるはずです」

増える美術館の提携

近年、コレクションの共有やリソースの集約、観客層の拡大を目指して提携を結ぶ美術館は増えている。その手法も、従来の短期的な作品貸借から、共同購入や個人からの共同寄贈、地域ネットワークの構築、長期的な国際交流など、より踏み込んだモデルへと進化してきた。共同購入は、2003年に ホイットニー美術館 、 テート 、ポンピドゥー・センターの3館がビル・ヴィオラの映像インスタレーション『Five Angels for the Millennium』を 共同収蔵して以来 、ますます一般的になっている。

今回の3館のモデルに近い前例としては、2018年に中国系インドネシア人コレクターのブディ・テックが、 ロサンゼルス・カウンティ美術館（LACMA） および自身が上海に設立した余徳耀美術館（ユズ・ミュージアム）との間で結んだコレクション共有の枠組みがある（中国政府は余徳耀美術館の公立化を認めず、 テックは2022年に死去 ）。このケースでは新たな財団が設立され、作品を中国に保管しつつ、ロサンゼルスと上海を行き来させて企画展を行う仕組みがとられた。例えば2019年にはLACMAの所蔵品が「In Production: Art and the Studio System」展として余徳耀美術館に巡回し、2021年にはテックのコレクションから20点がLACMAの「Legacies of Exchange」展で公開された。

さらに最近では、特定のコレクターの所蔵品を複数の美術館で共同管理するケースも相次いでいる。2022年には、ギリシャの実業家ディミトリ・ダスカロプーロスのコレクションから約100点が、 ソロモン・R・グッゲンハイム美術館 と シカゴ現代美術館 に共同寄贈された。2024年には、ハマー美術館、LACMA、 ロサンゼルス現代美術館（MOCA） の3館が、ジャール＆パメラ・モーン夫妻から約350点の共同寄贈を受けている。これら3館は現在も、モーン・アート・コレクティブ（MAC3）と名付けられたこのコレクションの拡充を続けている。（翻訳：編集部）

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Head Gear Films is opening in the U.S. and company co-founder and CEO Phil Hunt has told Deadline Head Gear US will sink $120M into U.S. indie film and TV in year one.

Head Gear exec Samantha Allwinton will run the new unit as Director of Operations. She will be based in Denver and spend time between there and LA. She was previously COO of Head Gear Films, based in London. Before joining Head Gear she was at Ingenious Media.

Head Gear majors in independent film, TV and games finance, including government incentives, presales, gap and bridge funding, as well as executive production and packaging. It has recently helped finance The Apprentice , Talk to Me and How to Have Sex .

Related Stories

New AFM Summit To Explore Federal Production Tax Incentive

Federal Film & TV Tax Credit Bill Adds Eight New Senate Co-Sponsors

The Head Gear US office is opening its doors as a new proposed federal tax credit, part of the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, is moving through Congress. It would apply on top of new and existing state-level incentives.

Watch on Deadline

Hunt said he wants Head Gear to be in position as the aforementioned industry-boosting measures take effect, which he expects to happen by year-end. “Over 50% of our deal flow is American movies, so we’ve already laid that down. The reason to go to LA is to increase that flow because the federal tax credit’s coming in, which is nice timing. It’s about having more of a foothold in the U.S. and being on their time zone.”

He added: “U.S. producers will have half their budget covered and still need the rest. We’ve closed that gap on close to 600 films. We want to be there before the rush.”

Head Gear is using existing resources for its U.S. expansion and will provide various types of finance. “When we look at where the company is at right now, and all the other companies that we’re horizontally integrated into, they’re growing. We have got money that we can deploy,” Hunt said.

The Head Gear team are regular visitors to the U.S. and Hunt made the point that having a full-fledged base there has been a long-held ambition. “I’ve been meaning to open up in the States for a very long time. I’ve never found the right person until now, who’s got exactly what Head Gear needs and understands Head Gear’s character and ethos, which is quite different from that of most people.”

The newly-minted Head Gear US will be at AFM in November and then Sundance in January. “I’ve spent years running Head Gear from the inside,” said Allwinton. “I know how we choose films and why we say no to most of them.

“Now I get to sit across the table from U.S. producers and tell them straight what their film is worth and how we’d get it made. American independents are about to get a lot of new money. We’re here to help them turn it into films people buy.”

Production Focus

Hunt co-founded Head Gear in 2002 with Compton Ross, who as well as his film interests has been a CEO in the international oil and gas industry for 48 years.

With the U.S. office opening, Hunt also spoke about his wider strategy for the business and plans to boost Head Gear’s production-side role.

“We’ve been silently kind of working on the production side of Head Gear, and the next phase for us as a business is going back into production and really kind of being the producer’s producer. So, working for the producer in the background; they’ve developed projects, and then we help package them up, do the business affairs, get them off the ground, run finance plans, and then years down the line, we’re still helping collect the money.”

Hunt said Head Gear is helping to fund about 30 movies a year and is a hands-on exec producer on a third of those. “Coming from a ‘failed’ producer background, I’m really fascinated with helping producers and guiding them through the marketplace better than ever using our data.”

Source: HanWay Films / MetFilm Distribution

‘Extra Geography’, ‘Effi o Blaenau’

Actors from Extra Geography , Effi o Blaenau , Animol and Sunny Dancer are among the 14 UK talents on the British Independent Film Awards (Bifa) breakthrough performance longlist for 2026.

The actors highlighted for their performances in new UK independent features include Galaxie Clear and Marni Duggan, leads in Molly Manners’ Extra Geography , about two teenage girls at an English boarding school who make it their summer project to fall in love.

Scroll down for the full longlist

Tut Nyuot and Sekou Diaby both make the list for their performances in Ashley Walters’ directorial debut Animol , set in a juvenile detention centre where young inmates navigate the harsh realities while attempting to find redemption.

Also selected are Leisa Gwenllian for her role in Marc Evans’ Effi o Blaenau , about a young woman living in a slate quarry town in Wales; and Daniel Quinn-Toye for George Jaques’ teenage cancer survivor camp drama Sunny Dancer .

Eight of the longlisted actors have previously been selected as Screen UK and Ireland Stars of Tomorrow: Galaxie Clear , Sekou Diaby , Leisa Gwenllian , Jonathan Jules (all 2026); Tut Nyuot , Daniel Quinn-Toye (2025), Florence Hunt (2024) and Laurie Kynaston (2018). Séamus McLean Ross was named in the Rising Stars Scotland showcase in 2024.

The actors all qualify for Bifa’s six-month Breakthrough Performers Programme, offering sessions covering career development, wellbeing, casting, financial literacy and networking opportunities.

Previous winners of the award include Ben Whishaw, Jamie Bell, Naomi Ackie, Dev Patel, Jessie Buckley, Walters, and last year’s recipient Posy Sterling for Lollipop .

The breakthrough performance longlist follows yesterday’s cinema of the year list. The nominees will be announced on Tuesday, November 3; with the winners revealed at the Bifa ceremony at London’s Camden Roundhouse on Sunday, December 6.

Bifa Breakthrough Performance longlist 2026

Galaxie Clear, Extra Geography

Sekou Diaby, Animol

Marni Duggan, Extra Geography

Olive Gray, Surviving Earth

Joshua Griffin, Masc

Leisa Gwenllian, Effi o Blaenau

Florence Hunt, Queen At Sea

Jonathan Jules, Florid

Laurie Kynaston, Lady

Chirag Benedict Lobo, The Cycle Of Love

Séamus McLean Ross, California Schemin’

Tut Nyuot, Animol

Daniel Quinn-Toye, Sunny Dancer

Luke Tittensor, Straight Circle

article_text:
Archives – October 15, 2021

Galerie Bene Taschen will be presenting the Hardened project by Jeff Mermelstein in the form of a solo exhibition.

Jeff Mermelstein, born 1957 in New Jersey, has left decades of work with a Leica camera behind him and made the switch to the camera on his iPhone. In his series Hardened, Mermelstein has rediscovered street photography in the age of social media, through unconventional compositions and bizarre objects.

In this digital age, people portray themselves as street photographers on social networks. Even Mermelstein posts his pictures on Instagram and thus embraces this trend.

Mermelstein is a master of camouflage; he shoots under cover as a voyeur, capturing intimate and absurd moments. The close-up of a man taking a bite out of a peach reveals each and every pore of his face and leads the viewer into his private sphere. Animals, people and objects are, in turn, distorted by blurred details.

Pixelated and blurred objects come to the fore, for instance, the glittering surface of a skateboard, which can only be discerned as such by those in the know. The planes of the image merge, and can only be distinguished from one another and deciphered through close observation. And so, what appears to be a bright tunnel turns out to be the inside of a paper cup filled with some kind of dark soft drink.

Jeff Mermelstein’s street photography reveals understated similarities, such as the identical hues of a carrot salad and the embroidery on the shirt of the person eating it. At the same time, it focuses on details that, through its extreme magnification, seem to violate the privacy of the people depicted and reveal every flaw.

The book of the same name, Hardened by Jeff Mermelstein, was published by Mörel Verlag in 2019.

Jeff Mermelstein : Hardened

16 October – 4 December 2021

Galerie Bene Taschen

Moltkestraße 81

50674 Cologne

www.benetaschen.com

連続テレビ小説「ブラッサム」

＜総合＞【毎週月曜～土曜】 午前8時～8時15分＊土曜は1週間を振り返ります ＜NHK BS＞【毎週月曜～金曜】午前7時30分～7時45分 ＜BSP4K＞【毎週月曜～金曜】午前7時30分～7時45分

【作】 櫻井 剛、小松與志子 【音楽】 fox capture plan 【主題歌】 「咲き誇れ」 YOASOBI 【出演】 石橋静河、加賀まりこ、松たか子、国仲涼子、渡部篤郎 ほか 【スタッフ】 制作統括：村山峻平、櫻井壮一 プロデューサー：大野陽平 演出：盆子原 誠、中泉 慧、佐藤玲衣、田中陽児、小林直毅、野田雄介

公式サイト 公式X 公式Instagram

第５週 「狂騒で、東京」

東京・本郷で、珠（石橋静河）と保（金子大地）は、下宿の大家に自分たちが兄妹だと嘘をつきながら同居していた。保は大学に通い、珠は保の世話と家事をする暮らし。そんな中、珠は近所の書店で、若手一番の作家、秋山格之介（高良健吾）や「イワンの馬鹿」を翻訳した作家、小山牛丸（イッセー尾形）と出会い、大きな刺激を受ける。そんな中、下宿の大家の娘・三好マキ（中村優子）が、珠と保は兄妹ではないと疑い始める…。

あわせて読みたい
